title: Optimal transport unlocks end-to-end learning for single-molecule localization
one_liner: Replace non-differentiable filtering with optimal transport loss to enable end-to-end learning for dense fluorescence microscopy.
lead: Single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM) reconstructs tiny cellular structures by finding thousands of tagged molecules in images. Current methods rely on non-differentiable layers that discard molecules, breaking the training pipeline. This paper uses a mathematical tool called optimal transport to match predicted and real molecules end-to-end, enabling training at high densities where molecules overlap.

problem.h2: The microscope sees crowded molecules but training breaks
paras: A fluorescence microscope tags molecules with glowing dyes, then images them. Each glowing spot reveals a molecule's position. To get accurate positions, microscopes wait until most dyes are dark and only a few are glowing at once, then fire the camera. This produces slow, non-overlapping images.

A beginner might think: train a neural network directly on the raw microscope image to predict molecule positions everywhere at once. The problem is that the network is trained by comparing its predicted positions to the ground-truth positions, but the training objective only looks at individual pixels—it does not care about matching predicted molecules to real molecules. Then at inference time, the code uses a handcrafted filter called non-maximum suppression (NMS) to pick the strongest spots and discard overlapping ones. NMS is not differentiable—it is a hard decision gate that does not feed learning signals back into the network weights. This breaks end-to-end learning. And because NMS discards any detection too close to a stronger neighbor, it can discard real molecules.

callout.html: Replace the pixel-wise training loss and the non-differentiable NMS filter with a differentiable loss that directly matches predicted and real molecules.

hidden.h2: The assignment cost: which predicted spot is which real spot
hidden.name: optimal assignment distance
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity: the total distance cost of the best one-to-one matching between predicted molecules and real molecules. This is not pixel overlap or per-pixel error; it is the sum of distances in the assignment that minimizes total travel. For example, if you predict spots at positions 1, 5, and 9, and the real molecules are at positions 2, 6, and 10, the optimal matching pairs each prediction to its nearest real molecule: prediction 1 to real 2 costs distance 1, prediction 5 to real 6 costs distance 1, prediction 9 to real 10 costs distance 1, for a total cost of 3. A different pairing, like prediction 1 to real 6, prediction 5 to real 2, prediction 9 to real 10, would cost 5 plus 3 plus 1, which totals 9, so the algorithm avoids it.

The paper estimates this using the Sinkhorn algorithm, a smooth iterative procedure that solves the assignment problem while keeping all derivatives alive. During training, the network learns to place predictions that minimize this total distance, automatically learning the best strategy for overlapping molecules.

heat.caption: Darker means higher cost in the optimal transport distance table.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the minimum total distance to pair up every predicted spot with a real molecule. Lower is better because it means the network's predictions are close to the true molecule positions.

Optimal transport solves for the assignment pattern that minimizes the total distance to the cost matrix, with a smoothing term (entropy penalty) that keeps learning signals smooth and prevents hard, non-differentiable decisions.

paras: The old approach broke because it trained pixel-by-pixel (each location independent) but tested with a global filter (NMS, which depends on neighbors). The network had no way to learn what the filter would do.

This paper uses optimal transport to make training and testing speak the same language. During training, the loss measures: given my predicted set of molecule positions, how far is it from the ground-truth set? The answer is the minimum cost to pair them up. This cost is computed using the Sinkhorn algorithm, a smooth iterative method that preserves gradients all the way back to the network weights. At inference, the network simply outputs its predicted positions and a threshold filters by confidence—no NMS needed, no gradient break.

math.words: loss equals the inner product of the optimal assignment and the distance cost matrix, where the assignment solves a regularized transport problem using the Sinkhorn algorithm
math.equation: L = trace(Gamma_star^T * C), where Gamma_star solves: arg min_Gamma [trace(Gamma^T * C) - epsilon * H(Gamma)]
symbols: the optimal assignment matrix (rows = predictions, columns = real molecules; exactly one 1 per row and column)
cost matrix where C[i,j] = distance from predicted spot i to real spot j
entropy of the assignment (encourages smoothness, not hard 0-1)
regularization strength that trades off optimality for smoothness (higher epsilon means smoother gradients)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say the network predicts spots at positions [0, 5] and real molecules are at [1, 6].
Cost matrix C = [[1, 6], [5, 1]]. (distance from pred-0 to real-1 is 1, to real-6 is 6, etc.)
Optimal assignment: pair pred-0 with real-1 (cost 1) and pred-5 with real-6 (cost 1). Total cost = 2.
Wrong assignment: pair pred-0 with real-6 (cost 6) and pred-5 with real-1 (cost 5). Total cost = 11.
The algorithm avoids the wrong pairing. The loss L = 2 tells the network to keep outputting positions close to [1, 6].

math.note: The Sinkhorn algorithm solves this efficiently in a few iterations, and every iteration is differentiable, so gradients flow back through the matching decision.

charts.title: Old approach (pixel loss + NMS)
charts.note: NMS loses true positives when spots overlap. Non-differentiable filter blocks gradient learning.

charts.title: This paper (optimal transport loss + simple threshold)
charts.note: All predictions learned end-to-end. Gracefully handles overlap because matching is global, not local.

items.b: False negatives if smoothing is too weak.
items.html: If the smoothing strength is set too low, the Sinkhorn algorithm finds a hard assignment too quickly. The network learns to output only the closest spots and ignores distant molecules, which the loss then penalizes. Setting smoothing too high smooths away the distinctions. Trade-off required.

items.b: Ghost predictions when molecule count is uncertain.
items.html: The loss assumes the network knows exactly how many real molecules are in the frame. If the network outputs more or fewer predictions than there are ground-truth molecules, the optimal transport will match some predictions to nothing or some real molecules to nothing (padded with a fixed-cost dummy slot). The paper does not fully address how to learn the molecule count from data.

The paper proposes iterating the encoder-decoder K times, refining predictions each iteration. This is expensive at inference. For real-time live-cell imaging, a simpler single-pass variant may be needed.

When the network knows the frame size and the ground-truth molecule count, optimal transport directly trains it to place predictions close to real molecules. No hand-crafted filters, no gradient breaks.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy microscope simulator that renders overlapping glowing spots at known positions. Train a small encoder-decoder network using the optimal transport loss (not pixel-wise loss, not NMS). At inference, output positions and filter by confidence. Compare accuracy on dense frames (many overlapping molecules) to a baseline that uses pixel loss and NMS.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = (number of correctly paired predictions) / (total real molecules). Test on high-density frames where molecules overlap.
demo.closing: The demo must show that optimal transport learns to resolve overlapping molecules where NMS fails, and that gradients flow end-to-end without freezing at a filter.
